newsitem.title: USA: House Republicans write immigrant welfare policy.
newsitem.headline: House Republicans write immigrant welfare policy.

text.p: House Republicans Tuesday jettisoned a deal worked out with the White House preserving federal aid for disabled legal immigrants.

As part of legislation to implement the welfare provisions of a five-year balanced budget deal, Republicans also intended to soften a recent White House ruling that welfare recipients in workfare programs must be paid the minimum wage.
The legislation will be officially unveiled Wednesday.

A landmark welfare bill signed by President Clinton last year ends federal benefits to most legal immigrants this summer. The White House tried to "fix" the welfare bill as part of a budget deal worked out with Republicans last month.

Under the original budget plan, legal immigrants who were in the United States by August 22, 1996, and were either on the rolls or became disabled could continue aid. Some disabled immigrants who entered after that date could also receive aid, according to the House budget resolution.
Immigrants who received federal help because they are elderly and impoverished, rather than disabled, would have been cut off this summer.

Under the new Republican plan, all legal immigrants -- including the poor -- who were receiving federal help through the Social Security system on August 22, 1996, could continue aid. No other legal immigrants would be eligible.
Immigrants who had official sponsors with incomes above 150 percent of the poverty line, however, would be cut off.

"I think our (plan) is much more humane. The way the president wants to go, people would actually be pushed out of nursing homes," said Florida Republican Rep. Clay Shaw, the chief author of the legislation.
Advocates for the poor said Congress should focus aid on disabled immigrants, who were the most vulnerable, and crticized the proposal to cut off individuals with sponsors.

"It clearly violates the specific policy agreement that was reached by the White House and congressional Republican leaders," said Ellen Nissenbaum of the liberal Center on Budget and Policy Priorities.
"It not only reverses the priorities, it even restricts or will eliminate protection for some who were already covered," she said.

The new bill also softens a White House ruling that welfare recipients in mandatory work programs are eligible for the minimum wage. Govenors have complained that would make it too expensive for them to implement work programs.
The Republican proposal would allow states to count Food Stamps, Medicaid, housing assistance and other benefits as income.
In one area of bipartisan agreement, the legislation includes $3 billion in grants to help create jobs in impoverished regions of the country.
